items.title: Karma's Classification Opens: The Ten Wholesome and Ten Unwholesome Courses of Action

items.zh: 業分別云何？謂由二種相應知。一、由補特伽羅相差別故；二、由法相差別故。此復二種，即善、不善十種業道。
items.en: What is the classification of karma? It should be understood through two aspects: first, through the differing character of the person who performs it; second, through the differing character of the deed's own nature. This latter, in turn, comprises two sets: the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome courses of action.

items.zh: 所謂殺生，離殺生；不與取，離不與取；欲邪行，離欲邪行；妄語，離妄語；離間語，離離間語；麁惡語，離麁惡語；綺語，離綺語；貪欲，離貪欲；瞋恚，離瞋恚；邪見，離邪見。
items.en: Namely: killing, and abstaining from killing; taking what is not given, and abstaining from it; sexual misconduct, and abstaining from it; false speech, and abstaining from it; divisive speech, and abstaining from it; harsh speech, and abstaining from it; frivolous speech, and abstaining from it; covetousness, and abstaining from it; ill will, and abstaining from it; wrong view, and abstaining from it.

items.title: The Killer's Psychological Portrait, and Why No Life Falls Outside Compassion's Reach

items.zh: 補特伽羅相差別建立者，謂如經言：諸殺生者，乃至廣說。殺生者者，此是總句。最極暴惡者，謂殺害心正現前故。血塗其手者，謂為成殺，身相變故。害極害執者，謂斷彼命故，解支節故，計活命故。無有羞恥者，謂自罪生故。無有哀愍者，謂引彼非愛故。
items.en: As for establishing differences by the character of the person: as the sūtra says of killers, stated in full. "Utterly savage" means the intention to kill stands directly present before the mind. "Hands smeared with blood" means the body's very appearance is transformed in the act of accomplishing the killing. "Harming, extreme harming, and clinging to it" means taking a life, dismembering the body limb from limb, and adopting killing itself as one's livelihood. "Without shame" means the guilt is self-inflicted and unacknowledged. "Without compassion" means bringing about what is thoroughly unwanted for another.

items.zh: 有出家外道，名曰無繫，彼作是說：百踰繕那內所有眾生，於彼律儀，若不律儀。為治彼故，說如是言：一切有情所。即彼外道復作是說：樹等外物亦有生命。為治彼故，說如是言：真實眾生所。
items.en: There is a non-Buddhist renunciant order called the Unbound, who hold: towards the beings within a hundred yojanas, there is either moral restraint or its absence. To counter this, the scripture says: towards all sentient beings. That same order further holds: trees and other external things likewise possess life. To counter this, the scripture says: towards genuinely sentient beings.

items.zh: 此即顯示真實福德遠離對治，及顯示不實福德遠離對治。如是所說諸句，顯示加行殺害。
items.en: This shows the antidote that keeps one from genuine merit, and the antidote that keeps one from merit that is not genuine. The phrases stated thus show killing at the stage of preparation.

items.title: Indiscriminate Killing, the Door Still Open to Change, and a Story of Fleas Left Unharmed

items.zh: 乃至極下捃多蟻等諸眾生所者，此句顯示無擇殺害。於殺生事若未遠離者，此顯遇緣容可出離。謂乃至未遠離來，名殺生者。
items.en: "Down to the very lowest, even ants and the like" — this phrase shows killing with no discrimination at all. "As long as one has not yet abandoned the act of killing" — this shows that, given the right conditions, one may still turn away from it. That is: only up until one has actually abandoned it does one continue to be called a killer.

items.zh: 又此諸句略義者，謂為顯示殺生相貌、殺生作用、殺生因緣，及與殺生事用差別。又略義者，謂為顯示殺生如實、殺生差別、殺所殺生、名殺生者。又此諸句，顯能殺生補特伽羅相，非顯殺生法相。復次，
items.en: Further, the summary meaning of these phrases is that they show the appearance of killing, the function of killing, the conditions of killing, and the different kinds of act and use in killing. Again, the summary meaning is that they show killing as it really is, the varieties of killing, the being that is killed, and the one who is called a killer. Further, these phrases show the characteristics of the person who kills, not the characteristics of killing as a dharma. Further,

items.title: Theft's Fourteen-Part Anatomy: What Actually Counts as Taking What Is Not Given

items.zh: 不與取者者，此是總句。於他所有者，謂他所攝財穀等事。若在聚落者，謂即彼事於聚落中若積集、若移轉。若閑靜處者，謂即彼事於閑靜處，若生、若集，或復移轉。即此名為可盜物數者，謂所不與、不捨、不棄物。
items.en: "One who takes what is not given" is the summary phrase. "Belonging to another" means wealth, grain, or similar goods that belong to someone else. "Within a settlement" means that very item, within a settlement, being either gathered together or moved elsewhere. "Within a secluded place" means that very item, within a secluded place, whether growing, gathered, or moved elsewhere. "What counts as stealable" refers to what its owner has not given, not relinquished, and not discarded.

items.zh: 若自執受者，謂執為己有。不與而取者，謂彼或時資具闕少，執為己有。不與而樂者，謂樂受行偷盜事業。於所不與、不捨、不棄而生希望者，謂劫盜他欲為己有。
items.en: "Claiming it for oneself" means taking hold of it as one's own possession. "Taking without it being given" means that, lacking some necessity, one appropriates it as one's own. "Delighting in taking without it being given" means taking pleasure in the very activity of stealing. "Harbouring a hope towards what has not been given, relinquished, or discarded" means intending to seize what belongs to another and make it one's own.

items.title: Theft's Remaining Elements, and How the Portraits of Wrongdoing Actually Work

items.zh: 若彼物主非先所與，如酬債法，是名不與。若彼物主於彼取者而不捨與，是名不捨。若彼物主於諸眾生不隨所欲受用而棄，是名不棄。自為而取者，謂不與而取故，及不與而樂故。饕餮而取者，謂所不與、不捨、不棄而希望故。
items.en: "Not given" means the owner never originally intended to give it, yet is compelled to hand it over as though repaying a debt. "Not relinquished" means the owner, even towards the one taking it, has not actually released it. "Not discarded" means the owner has not abandoned it for anyone at all who might wish to use it. "Taking on one's own initiative" means taking it without it being given, and delighting in doing so. "Taking with sheer greed" means harbouring the desire for what has been neither given, relinquished, nor discarded.

items.zh: 不清而取者，謂於所競物為他所勝，不清雪故。不淨而取者，謂雖勝他，而為過失垢所染故。有罪而取者，謂能攝受現法、後法非愛果故。於不與取若未遠離者，如前殺生相說應知。
items.en: "Taking without vindication" means, in a dispute over a contested item, losing to another party and failing to clear one's own claim. "Taking with impurity" means winning such a dispute, yet through means tainted by wrongdoing. "Taking that is criminal" means an act that draws an undesired result, both in this present life and in lives to come. "Not yet having abandoned taking what is not given" should be understood exactly as with the killer described above.

items.zh: 所餘業道亦爾。此中略義者，謂由盜此故成不與取、若於是處如其差別、如實劫盜，由劫盜故得此過失，是名總義。
items.en: The remaining courses of action are likewise. The summary meaning here is: by stealing this, one commits taking what is not given; in that place, according to its variety, one actually robs; and through robbing one incurs this fault. This is the general meaning.

items.zh: 又此中亦顯不與取者相，非不與取法相。當知餘亦爾。
items.en: What has been shown here, too, is the character of the person who takes what is not given — not the abstract nature of the deed of taking itself. The same should be understood to hold for every remaining course of action as well.

items.zh: 復次，欲邪行者者，此是總句。
items.en: Further, 'one who engages in sexual misconduct' is the general phrase.

items.title: Sexual Misconduct Opens: Who Falls Under Another's Protection

items.zh: 於諸父母等所守護者，猶如父母於己處女，為適事他故，勤加守護，時時觀察，不令與餘共為鄙穢。若彼沒已，復為至親兄弟姊妹之所守護。此若無者，復為餘親之所守護。此若無者，恐損家族，便自守護。或彼舅姑，為自兒故，勤加守護。
items.en: "Under the protection of parents and the like": just as parents diligently protect their own unmarried daughter, watching over her constantly so that she may properly be given in marriage, and do not allow her to be defiled with another. Should the parents have passed away, she is then protected by her closest siblings. Lacking these, she is protected by more distant relatives. Lacking these too, fearing harm to her family's honour, she protects herself. Or her future parents-in-law, for the sake of their own son, diligently protect her.

items.zh: 有治罰者，謂諸國王，若執理者，以治罰法而守護故。有障礙者，謂守門者所守護故。此中略顯未適他者三種守護。一、尊重至親眷屬自己之所守護，二、王執理家之所守護，三、諸守門者之所守護。
items.en: "Under legal protection": kings and magistrates protect her by means of the law's penalties. "Under physical safeguard": gatekeepers protect her by their watch. This briefly shows three kinds of protection for an unmarried woman: first, protection by revered close relatives or by herself; second, protection by the king or ruling authority; third, protection by those who guard the gate.

blocks.text: The treatise now describes the ten unwholesome courses of action in a distinctive way: not by defining the deed, but by drawing a portrait of the person who does it, phrase by phrase from a sūtra passage. It says so explicitly at the end of the account of theft. This makes the reading unusually human. Today: killing and taking what is not given.

Karma is classified by the character of the person and by the nature of the deed. The ten courses are: killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view, and their ten opposites. Today and tomorrow the treatise uses the first lens; on Day 59 it returns to define each deed's formal nature.

The sūtra phrase describes the killer as "cruel, with bloodied hands, engaged in harming, extreme harming, and clinging". Master Cháng Bǎi, following the *Pīxún jì*: taking life is "harming", dismembering is "extreme harming", making a living by killing is "clinging".

Two phrases answer other schools. The Nirgranthas held that restraint applies only to beings within a hundred yojanas; the sūtra says "**towards all sentient beings**". They also held that trees have life; the sūtra says "towards *genuinely sentient* beings". Trees have no likes or dislikes, so not harming them is not the precept against killing.
"Down to the very lowest, even ants": Master Cháng Bǎi explains the rare word 捃多 as an ant with broken legs, or ant eggs. No life is too small to fall within compassion.

subs.head: Indiscriminate killing, and the door still open

blocks.text: Some kill without discrimination. Yet even the killer "may still turn away given the right conditions". Master Cháng Bǎi tells of a man who from childhood never killed; when changing his clothes he picked out even the fleas and set them elsewhere. When he stayed three days in others' rooms, it was said, the fleas left of their own accord. The point is not the miracle but the claim that habits of harmlessness grow, as Day 54's habituation said.

Theft is described in fourteen phrases. "What counts as stealable" is what "its owner has not given, not relinquished, and not discarded". Venerable Miào Jìng: in the monastic code the offence is complete "when it is lifted from its place".

The list covers things in villages and in secluded places, "whether growing or gathered". Master Cháng Bǎi's modern reminder: "Visiting a national park or the beach, you shouldn't bring home plants or stones." Things in wild places may seem to belong to no one, but they do.

"Taking with impurity" means winning a dispute over something and keeping it. Master Cháng Bǎi: if it is not truly yours and you out-argue the owner, the acquisition is impure; Venerable Miào Jìng: even out-arguing someone this way is still taking what is not given.

Then the treatise's methodological note: "What has been shown here is the character of the person who takes what is not given, not the abstract nature of the deed itself. The same should be understood for every course of action." The portraits are meant to help us recognise the tendencies in ourselves before they become deeds.
The third course opens with who falls under another's protection: married women, and unmarried women protected by their family, by the law, or by guardians. Tomorrow the treatise completes it.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, through what two aspects is karma classified, and what does the "deed's own nature" comprise?
options: by the person's character and by the deed's nature; the latter comprises the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome courses
quiz.why: "First, through the differing character of the person who performs it; second, through the differing character of the deed's own nature. This latter, in turn, comprises two sets: the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome courses of action." §26–48 treat the person, §49–51 the deed. Venerable Miào Jìng: "this" may cover both person and deed.

quiz.q: According to Master Cháng Bǎi, why is karma called a "course" or "path" (業道)?
options: the ten evils lead to the lower realms, the ten goods to humans and gods — karma is a road
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "The ten evil deeds lead to the three lower realms; the ten good deeds lead to humans and gods — so karma is a path, called a course of action." The pudgala is the one who repeatedly takes up results in the five destinies.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what do the Nirgranthas hold, and which scriptural phrase counters it?
options: restraint applies only to beings within a hundred yojanas; the sūtra counters with "towards all sentient beings"
quiz.why: "They hold: within a hundred yojanas of where one dwells, restraint from killing constitutes moral discipline … To counter this, the scripture says: towards all sentient beings." Master Cháng Bǎi: a hundred yojanas is about 1,600 li (one yojana = 16 li). (The reading note's "a thousand miles" overstates it.)

quiz.q: "Down to the very lowest, even 捃多 ants" — how do the teachers explain 捃多蟻?
options: an ant with broken legs; ant eggs are also called this
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "An ant with broken legs is called a 捃多 ant; ant eggs are also so called." Venerable Miào Jìng agrees. The phrase shows "killing without discrimination" — sparing not even the smallest being.

quiz.q: The text says the killer "may still turn away given the right conditions." Master Cháng Bǎi tells a story about fleas. What happens?
options: someone who never killed from childhood moved even his fleas elsewhere when changing clothes; invited to stay three days in others' rooms, the fleas left — and the story doesn't say he was Buddhist
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "He couldn't bear to kill even the fleas on him; when changing or washing clothes, he picked them out and moved them elsewhere"; "people invited him to stay in their rooms three days, and afterwards the fleas were gone"; "it doesn't say he was a Buddhist — just that he never killed from childhood." Venerable Miào Jìng: meeting the Three Jewels' teaching, one may turn away.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what counts as "stealable"?
options: what the owner has not given, not relinquished, and not discarded
quiz.why: "'What counts as stealable' refers to what its owner has not given, not relinquished, and not discarded." §29 explains each. Master Cháng Bǎi: relinquishing usually has a specific recipient; discarding is towards everyone.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what do these phrases describe?
options: the character of the person who takes, not the deed's nature — and so for every course of action
quiz.why: "What has been shown here, too, is the character of the person who takes what is not given — not the abstract nature of the deed of taking itself. The same should be understood to hold for every remaining course of action." Master Cháng Bǎi: "This shows the person, not the deed." The deed's nature comes in §49 on.
